the fibroblast derived extracellular matrix, termed cardiogel, is superior to commercial matrices of laminin and fibroblasts in supporting the earliest maturation of the neonatal cardiomyocyte, in terms of physical growth, spontaneous contractile activity, calcium handling efficiency and development of a key subcellular organnelle, the mitochondria.

cardiogel, a fibroblast derived extracellular matrix, supports the earliest development of spontaneous contractility and calcium handling in neonatal cardiac myocyte cultures, as compared to commercial laminin or fibronectin.
cardiogel, a fibroblast derived extracellular matrix, is the most supportive of neonatal rat cardiac cell growth and differentiation.

the development of a cardiac myocyte culture system, which will allow the study of cardiac function in the early stages of development and maturation.
the development of a more physiological model of the neonatal heart.
the effects of the extracellular matrix on cardiac myocyte growth and development, with emphasis on contractile and calcium transport properties.

neonatal cardiomyocyte growth, contractility, calcium handling and mitochondrial development are enhanced by the presence of a fibroblast derived matrix, as opposed to a single-component matrix.
the neonatal cardiac myocyte is able to respond to the presence of a fibroblast derived extracellular matrix by developing more rapidly than the cells grown on either laminin or fibronectin.

the cardiogeltissue matrix, which contains a mixture of laminin and fibroblast-derived proteins, is the most effective in supporting early maturation of neonatally isolated cardiomyocytes.

the cardiogell matrix is the most supportive matrix for neonatal rat cardiac cells.
